messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a step‑by‑step outline of how I would use the two tools you described to place an order for a burger and fries at McDonald’s. I’ll keep it high‑level so you can see the logical flow without getting bogged down in implementation details. --- ## 1. Discover the McDonald’s Ordering API | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **1.1** | Use the *search* tool to look for “McDonald’s online ordering API” or “McDonald’s mobile ordering API”. | We need to know whether McDonald’s exposes a public API and what its base URL is. | | **1.2** | Inspect the search results for official documentation, SDKs, or example calls. | Official docs give us the correct endpoints, required headers, auth flow, and data models. | | **1.3** | Identify the key endpoints we’ll need:
• `/locations` – to find a nearby store
• `/menu` – to fetch the menu items
• `/orders` – to create an order
• `/orders/{id}` – to check status | Knowing the endpoints lets us build the correct request URLs later. | --- ## 2. Find a Nearby McDonald’s Store | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **2.1** | Use the *search* tool to locate the “locations” endpoint (e.g., `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/locations`). | We need a specific store ID to place the order. | | **2.2** | Build a query string with your latitude/longitude (or ZIP code) to narrow the search. | The API will return a list of nearby stores; we’ll pick the nearest one. | | **2.3** | Execute the request via the *execute* tool and parse the JSON response. | The response contains store IDs, addresses, and operating hours. | | **2.4** | Pick the first store in the list (or the one with the best rating). | That store’s ID will be used in subsequent calls. | --- ## 3. Retrieve the Menu Items | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **3.1** | Use the *search* tool to locate the “menu” endpoint (e.g., `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu`). | We need to know the exact product IDs for a burger and fries. | | **3.2** | Build a request that includes the store ID from step 2. | The menu is often store‑specific (different sizes, add‑ons). | | **3.3** | Execute the request via the *execute* tool and parse the JSON. | The response lists all menu items with IDs, prices, and modifiers. | | **3.4** | Search the returned list for “burger” and “fries” (or “Big Mac”, “Medium Fries”). | We’ll capture the product IDs and any required modifiers (size, sauce). | | **3.5** | Record the product IDs and any default modifier IDs needed. | These IDs will be part of the order payload. | --- ## 4. Build the Order Payload | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **4.1** | Create a JSON object that follows the API’s order schema. | The API expects a specific structure (store ID, items, payment, delivery). | | **4.2** | Include the store ID from step 2. | Tells the system where to deliver. | | **4.3** | Add an array of items:
• Item 1: burger product ID + quantity 1
• Item 2: fries product ID + quantity 1 | These are the items you want. | | **4.4** | Add any required modifiers (e.g., size, sauce) that were identified in step 3. | Ensures the order matches the menu options. | | **4.5** | Add payment information (tokenized card, PayPal, etc.) or set “payment_method”: “pickup” if you’ll pay in‑store. | The API needs a payment method unless pickup is allowed. | | **4.6** | Add delivery or pickup details:
• For delivery: address, phone number
• For pickup: your name and phone number | The API needs contact info for confirmation. | | **4.7** | Validate the JSON against the schema (if a validator is available). | Prevents malformed requests. | --- ## 5. Submit the Order | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **5.1** | Use the *search* tool to confirm the “orders” POST endpoint (e.g., `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders`). | We need the exact URL and HTTP method. | | **5.2** | Build the request:
• Method: POST
• URL: orders endpoint
• Headers: `Content-Type: application/json`, `Authorization: Bearer ` (if required)
• Body: the JSON payload from step 4 | All the data we gathered is now sent to McDonald’s. | | **5.3** | Execute the request via the *execute* tool. | This creates the order. | | **5.4** | Parse the response:
• Success → order ID, estimated time, confirmation number
• Failure → error code, message | Gives us the order reference and next steps. | --- ## 6. Confirm & Track the Order | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **6.1** | If the response includes an order ID, use the *search* tool to locate the “order status” endpoint (e.g., `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders/{id}`). | Allows us to poll for updates. | | **6.2** | Build a GET request with the order ID and any required auth headers. | Retrieves the current state of the order. | | **6.3** | Execute the request via the *execute* tool and parse the status. | We can inform you when the order is ready or delivered. | | **6.4** | Optionally set up a polling loop (every 30 s) until status is “completed” or “delivered”. | Keeps you updated in real time. | --- ## 7. Handle Edge Cases & Errors | Scenario | What to do | Why it matters | |----------|------------|----------------| | **API rate limits** | Check response headers for `Retry-After` or `X-RateLimit-Reset`. | Avoids being blocked. | | **Payment declined** | Return the error message to the user and offer alternative payment methods. | Keeps the user informed. | | **Store closed** | Detect “closed” status in the locations response and suggest the next open store. | Provides a fallback. | | **Network failure** | Retry with exponential backoff or fall back to a cached menu. | Improves reliability. | --- ## 8. Wrap‑Up & Notify the User | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **8.1** | Send a confirmation message: “Your Big Mac and Medium Fries are on their way! Order #12345, ETA 15 min.” | Gives the user peace of mind. | | **8.2** | Offer a link or QR code to track the order in the McDonald’s app (if available). | Enhances user experience. | | **8.3** | Log the order details and any errors for future debugging. | Helps improve the system. | --- ### Summary Flow ``` Search → Find locations endpoint ↓ Execute → Get nearest store ID ↓ Search → Find menu endpoint ↓ Execute → Get menu items ↓ Parse → Identify burger & fries IDs ↓ Build → Order payload (store, items, payment, contact) ↓ Search → Find orders endpoint ↓ Execute → POST order ↓ Parse → Order ID & ETA ↓ Poll → Order status until completed ↓ Notify → User with confirmation & tracking link ``` --- That’s the complete pipeline. If you’d like me to actually perform any of these steps (e.g., search for the locations endpoint or submit the order), just let me know which step you’d like to start with and I’ll invoke the appropriate tool.
